title: RunPod Pricing 2026 for Pods, Serverless and Storage
summary: RunPod pricing charges per second for GPU time, with rates varying by GPU model and cloud tier. Determine costs for pods versus serverless.
body_markdown:
## Automating RunPod shutdowns and spend alerts with Activepieces


When a pod is forgotten, it keeps billing, and Activepieces can watch for it: a check that runs hourly is 720 runs in a 30-day month at 1 credit each, which fits inside the Free plan's 1,000 credits if you leave out the optional AI steps.


It can run a schedule, ask RunPod which pods are still up, stop the ones past a set time and tell your team, but it doesn't replace the controls RunPod already has.


### What RunPod already controls natively


Start with what the platform does itself, because a workflow you build on top should cover only what these leave open. RunPod lets you set an account-level spending limit and gives you balance-based alerts.


You can also set a pod to stop itself by ending the process it runs, so a job that finishes shuts its own pod down. That's the cleanest option, and it belongs inside the job script.


The gap is the pod nobody told to stop. A spend limit caps total damage, so a forgotten pod's cost has a ceiling. But the limit acts only after the money is gone and often blocks the work you wanted to keep running too.


A balance alert says the account is low, not which pod caused it. Neither one looks at a pod and asks whether it has been up longer than any job should take.


### A scheduled workflow that stops idle pods


That question is a clock check, and a clock check is what a scheduled flow does well. The flow below runs on a timer, fetches the list of pods from RunPod's API, loops through them, and compares each pod's start time against a cutoff.


It sends the old ones a stop request, then logs the result and emails the team.


The canvas shows the full chain: a schedule trigger feeding Google Sheets, a loop, a date helper, an HTTP request, two AI steps and a Sheets insert.


After that come a router with a Branch 1 path and an Otherwise path, and a Gmail send step.


Read the router as the decision point: pods past the cutoff go down one branch to be stopped and reported, everything else falls through untouched.


Of all the steps, the HTTP request matters most, since it calls RunPod's API directly, so you need an API key stored as a connection rather than pasted into the flow.


The AI steps are optional. They can write the alert in plain language, but the stop decision should rest on the date comparison, not on a model's judgment.


You don't have to build that chain by hand.


Describe it in Activepieces' built-in chat (list the pods past the cutoff, stop them, email the team) and what comes back is a live flow in your account, the same artifact a builder would have assembled, running under the same RBAC and audit logs as every other flow.


Its run trace shows each step's outcome, from the HTTP call to RunPod through the router to the Gmail send, so you can read exactly what happened on every run. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.


Be clear about the limits. The flow only helps if it runs, so a failed schedule leaves you back where you started. It also can't tell a pod that is training from one that is idle, because start time isn't activity.


If the cutoff sits below your longest legitimate job, you'll stop real work, so keep it above. Use it as a backstop to the job's own shutdown, not a substitute.
